screens.title: Architecting for Sustainability and Environmental Impact
screens.narratorSegment: As a solutions architect you are responsible for more than functionality and cost. You also design systems that use energy efficiently and reduce environmental impact. In this lesson you will learn core principles such as using only the resources you need, choosing power-efficient services, and minimizing unnecessary data movement. We will review right-sizing for compute and databases, explain why serverless and managed services often reduce idle power draw, and show storage and transfer strategies that lower energy use. You will also learn how to monitor impact with the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool and how to advise stakeholders on aligning architecture decisions with broader environmental, social, and governance objectives. By the end you will be able to propose practical changes — automated schedules for non-production, transitioning workloads to Graviton-based instances when appropriate, applying S3 lifecycle rules — and explain how these choices translate into reduced emissions. Consider how a small change, like turning off development instances overnight, directly reduces energy use and cost. What measurable change could your team make this week to reduce idle resource waste?

Architecting for Sustainability and Environmental Impact

Learn pragmatic design patterns and monitoring practices that reduce energy use and carbon emissions for cloud workloads. These ideas help you build systems that are efficient, cost-effective, and aligned with ESG goals.

Right-sizing
Identify over-provisioned compute and database resources; match capacity to real usage to cut waste and cost.
Power-efficient services

Measure & report

Coming up

We'll step through specific strategies, a Compute Optimizer lab scenario, and how to report emissions so you can advocate for sustainable architecture within your organization.

screens.title: Sustainable Architecture — Definition and Relevance
screens.narratorSegment: Sustainable architecture means designing, building, and operating cloud workloads with the explicit goal of minimizing environmental impact. That is more than a slogan: it means treating energy and data movement as design metrics alongside cost and latency. Architecturally, it starts with the principle 'use only the resources you need, when you need them.' Practically, that yields actions like right-sizing instances, scheduling non-production shutdowns, and choosing managed or serverless services that avoid idle power draw. A concrete example is a development environment that runs only during business hours. When you schedule those instances to stop overnight and on weekends, the instances consume no energy during those periods, producing immediate savings in both emissions and cost. A common misconception is that sustainability always requires expensive new hardware or complex change. In truth, many high-impact steps are operational: trimming unused snapshots, enabling S3 lifecycle transitions, and applying Compute Optimizer recommendations. Key takeaway: sustainability is measurable and actionable. Ask yourself: which idle resources in your account are easy candidates for shutdown or right-sizing this week? Sustainable Architecture — Definition and Relevance means sustainable architecture treats energy, data movement, and idle resources as first-class design concerns and applies practical patterns to reduce impact.. In practical terms, what it means to design cloud workloads for minimal environmental impact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Sustainable architecture treats energy, data movement, and idle resources as first-class design concerns and applies practical patterns to reduce impact.

content.html:
Core Concept › Sustainable Architecture

Definition and why it matters

Designing workloads to minimize environmental impact by reducing energy use, limiting unnecessary data movement, and using efficient services.

Key Takeaway

Sustainability is measurable: start with resource usage metrics and small operational changes that yield real impact.

Concrete example

A development cluster used only weekdays can be scheduled to stop at night and restart in the morning, eliminating idle energy and lowering monthly costs.

Common misconception

You don't always need new hardware to improve sustainability; operational changes and selecting efficient services often provide large wins.

Visual checklist
  • • Measure current usage: CPU, memory, network trends
  • • Identify idle or underutilized resources
  • • Apply right-sizing and schedule off-hours for non-prod
  • • Prefer serverless and managed services when feasible
  • • Use lifecycle policies to archive cold data
Try this

Pick one idle EC2 in your account, review its CloudWatch CPU and network metrics for 24 hours, and mark it as a candidate for scheduling or right-sizing.

screens.title: Right-sizing and Automated Schedules
screens.narratorSegment: Right-sizing and automated schedules are among the highest-impact operational steps architects can take. Start by collecting usage metrics such as C P U, memory, and network input and output over a representative period. Tools like AWS Compute Optimizer can analyze those metrics and propose smaller instance types when appropriate. A safe process is: identify candidates, simulate or test recommendations in non-production, and then apply changes during low-impact windows. For non-production environments that are only in use during business hours, implement automated shutdown and startup schedules. This can be done with scheduling tooling or simple automation that stops instances at night and restarts them in the morning. A concrete scenario: a t3. xlarge left running with low utilization for several days becomes a candidate for t3. medium or to be scheduled off when idle. The misconception to avoid is treating Compute Optimizer recommendations as automatic — always validate application behavior and performance after a change. Key takeaway: combine metrics, automated schedules, and safe validation to reduce running hours and energy consumption while preserving reliability. In practical terms, a step-by-step process to reduce idle compute and database waste. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Right-sizing & Schedules

Right-sizing workflow

  1. Measure: Collect 24–72 hours of CloudWatch metrics for candidate resources.
  2. Analyze: Use Compute Optimizer to surface over-provisioned instances and savings estimates.
  3. Test: Apply recommendations in a staging environment and validate performance.
  4. Apply: Schedule changes during maintenance windows and monitor post-change metrics.
  5. Automate: Implement schedules for non-production to stop instances off-hours.
Key Takeaway

Combining measurement, safe testing, and automation removes idle running hours and lowers both cost and emissions.

Example scenario
An m5.xlarge used only for light testing shows CPU under 10% most hours. Compute Optimizer suggests m5.large. After testing, you apply the change in staging and schedule the instance to stop at 7 PM and restart at 7 AM on weekdays.
Common mistake

Applying recommendations without testing can cause performance regressions. Validate before changing production configurations.

Pro tip

Start with non-production fleets for automated schedules — the savings are immediate and low risk.

screens.title: Graviton-Based Instances vs x86 — Power Efficiency Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing power-efficient instance types affects both performance and environmental impact. AWS offers ARM-based Graviton instances that often deliver better performance per watt than comparable x86 types. The practical decision requires workload validation. For C P U-bound workloads or highly parallel tasks, Graviton instances can provide similar or better throughput while consuming less energy for the same work. A contrasting scenario is software built and optimized only for x86 binaries; a migration could require recompilation or validation of libraries. A concrete example: an analytics service running many parallel worker processes may see improved throughput on M6g or C6g instances, translating into less runtime for the same job and therefore lower energy use. A common misconception is that switching is always a drop-in improvement. In reality, compatibility, performance profiles, and testing overhead matter. Key takeaway: consider Graviton for workloads that benefit from ARM architecture, but validate with benchmarks and performance testing so efficiency gains translate into real emissions reductions. keyIdea.title: Efficiency trade-off
keyIdea.text: Graviton instances can reduce energy per unit of work, but require validation for compatibility and workload profile before migration.

content.html:
Comparison › Graviton vs x86

When Graviton helps

  • • CPU-bound, parallel workloads often get better throughput per watt.
  • • Managed runtimes and modern toolchains usually support ARM without change.
  • • Lower energy per unit of work reduces emissions and cost when scaled.
Key Takeaway

Run benchmarks and compatibility tests. Efficiency gains must be measured in real workload terms to count as sustainability wins.

When x86 remains preferable

  • • Legacy binaries or closed-source dependencies that lack ARM builds.
  • • Specialized workloads tied to specific x86-optimized libraries.
  • • Migration costs or risk that outweigh measured efficiency benefits.
Concrete example

An analytics job on many cores ran 15% faster on M6g in benchmark tests, reducing total runtime and energy per job. But a legacy imaging pipeline required library changes and needed more validation before migrating.

screens.title: Serverless Computing and Sustainability
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless computing contributes to sustainability by shifting responsibility for capacity and efficiency to the cloud provider. In the serverless model you pay and consume only when your code runs. This eliminates long-lived idle capacity and reduces energy waste tied to always-on servers. Services such as Lambda, SQS, SNS, and DynamoDB are managed and scaled by the provider, which can optimize placement and power usage across many tenants. A concrete example is an event-driven image processing pipeline that runs only when images arrive; with Lambda, there is no always-on worker consuming C P U between events. A common misconception is that serverless is always cheaper or faster; in some high-throughput, long-running tasks, other models may be more cost-effective. The key sustainability insight is that serverless improves utilization and reduces idle draw. When designing, consider throughput patterns, cold start characteristics, and whether your workload maps naturally to event-driven scaling. A reflective question: which components of your systems are best matched to serverless to reduce idle energy use? Serverless Computing and Sustainability means serverless reduces idle power by running code only on demand, improving utilization and lowering emissions for event-driven workloads.. In practical terms, why serverless services often reduce idle energy consumption. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Serverless reduces idle power by running code only on demand, improving utilization and lowering emissions for event-driven workloads.

content.html:
Definition › Serverless Computing

Why serverless helps sustainability

Provider-managed scaling and pay-per-use execution reduce idle capacity and let infrastructure run at higher overall utilization.

When to use
Event-driven tasks, spiky workloads, lightweight compute bursts.
Watchouts
Long-running, stateful jobs may be better on dedicated compute.
Concrete example

An image ingestion service uses Lambda to resize images only when a new object is created. There are no idle workers consuming CPU between uploads, so energy per image is reduced.

Key Takeaway

Match workloads to serverless when demand is intermittent or event-driven to reduce idle resource consumption and improve efficiency.

screens.title: Data Transfer and Storage Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Data transfer and storage choices affect environmental impact because moving and storing data consumes energy. Start by minimizing cross-region and internet egress traffic where possible. Use caching and a content delivery network to reduce load on origin servers and avoid long-distance transfers. For storage, apply S3 intelligent tiering and lifecycle policies to transition objects to Glacier or Deep Archive as access patterns change. Deleting unnecessary data and old snapshots further reduces storage footprint and its associated energy cost. A concrete example is moving logs older than 90 days from S3 standard to Glacier Deep Archive, reducing the active storage footprint and the energy needed to replicate and maintain those objects. A common misconception is that cold data does not matter for sustainability. In reality, aggregated cold data across many buckets can represent a large and persistent energy cost. Key takeaway: design data flows to keep frequently accessed data close to users and age data into efficient storage tiers when it becomes infrequently accessed. Data Transfer and Storage Optimization means reduce cross-region transfers, cache with cloudfront, and transition cold data with lifecycle policies to lower energy and cost.. In practical terms, minimize unnecessary data movement and tier storage to reduce energy and cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Reduce cross-region transfers, cache with CloudFront, and transition cold data with lifecycle policies to lower energy and cost.

content.html:
Process Flow › Data Transfer & Storage

Practical steps

  1. Analyze traffic: Identify cross-region and internet egress hotspots.
  2. Cache: Use CloudFront to serve content closer to users and reduce origin load.
  3. Tier storage: Apply lifecycle rules to move cold data to Glacier classes.
  4. Clean up: Delete snapshots and unused objects regularly.
Key Takeaway

Architect to keep hot data nearby and move cold data to efficient tiers to lower storage energy and transfer costs.

Concrete example

Move log archives older than 90 days to Glacier Deep Archive using lifecycle rules and delete unattached snapshots to shrink storage footprint and reduce maintenance cost.

Common mistake

Assuming cold data has no impact. Aggregated cold storage adds ongoing energy and storage overhead that lifecycle rules can address.

screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring sustainability metrics lets architects convert technical decisions into measurable outcomes. AWS provides the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool in the console to visualize historical and projected carbon emissions related to your usage. Use the tool to see which services and accounts contribute most to the footprint and track changes over time when you apply right-sizing, lifecycle, or schedule policies. The practical workflow is to capture baseline emissions, implement optimization changes, and compare the tool's projected emissions to the baseline to demonstrate impact. A concrete example: after scheduling non-production instances off-hours and applying S3 lifecycle rules, you should observe a downward trend in projected emissions over subsequent reports. A common misconception is that usage metrics alone prove sustainability. You need the footprint visualization to connect resource changes to emissions. screens.title: Architecture Pattern: Serverless + Caching + Tiered Storage
screens.narratorSegment: A common sustainable architecture pattern combines serverless compute, caching at the edge, and tiered storage to minimize runtime and data transfer energy. The pattern serves content through a CDN, uses serverless functions for on-demand processing, and stores archival content in lower-cost, lower-energy storage classes. For example, a media delivery pipeline can use CloudFront to cache assets near users, Lambda for image resizing on demand, and S3 lifecycle rules to archive older versions to Glacier Deep Archive. This reduces long-distance transfers, eliminates always-on workers, and lowers active storage footprint. A misconception is that adding a CDN adds cost without environmental benefit. In practice, caching reduces origin load and cross-region egress, which lowers both cost and the energy footprint associated with repeated transfers. Key takeaway: combine serverless scaling with edge caching and lifecycle policies to reduce both runtime and storage energy while preserving user experience. In practical terms, a pattern that reduces runtime and transfer energy for user-facing content. Architecture › Serverless + CDN + Tiered Storage

Pattern components

  • • CloudFront caches content close to users to reduce origin requests.
  • • Lambda processes content on demand, eliminating always-on workers.
  • • S3 lifecycle rules move cold objects to Glacier classes for efficient storage.
Key Takeaway

This composition minimizes transfers and idle compute while preserving responsiveness through edge caching.

Concrete example

A media site uses CloudFront to cache thumbnails, Lambda to generate thumbnails only on first request, and archives raw footage to Glacier after 180 days. This reduces repeated origin processing and long-distance transfers.

Common mistake

Relying only on serverless without caching: on-demand processing for every request increases compute and transfer; combine both for best results.

fullNarratorScript:
As a solutions architect you are responsible for more than functionality and cost. You also design systems that use energy efficiently and reduce environmental impact. In this lesson you will learn core principles such as using only the resources you need, choosing power-efficient services, and minimizing unnecessary data movement. We will review right-sizing for compute and databases, explain why serverless and managed services often reduce idle power draw, and show storage and transfer strategies that lower energy use. You will also learn how to monitor impact with the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool and how to advise stakeholders on aligning architecture decisions with broader environmental, social, and governance objectives. By the end you will be able to propose practical changes — automated schedules for non-production, transitioning workloads to Graviton-based instances when appropriate, applying S3 lifecycle rules — and explain how these choices translate into reduced emissions. Consider how a small change, like turning off development instances overnight, directly reduces energy use and cost. What measurable change could your team make this week to reduce idle resource waste?

These objectives will guide your practical work as a solutions architect focused on sustainability. First, you will understand the principles of sustainable architecture in the cloud and why environmental responsibility matters alongside cost and performance. That means learning to think about energy use, idle resources, and data movement as measurable design factors. Second, you will identify AWS services and design patterns that reduce carbon footprint, including serverless, managed services, and Graviton-based instance types. Third, you will implement strategies such as right-sizing, automated schedules, lifecycle policies, and efficient data transfer to minimize environmental impact in real workloads. Fourth, you will use AWS tools — notably the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool — to monitor and report sustainability metrics and align technical decisions with broader ESG goals. Each objective combines a practical task and a reporting skill so you can both act and demonstrate impact to stakeholders. By practicing these skills you will be equipped to propose changes that save energy, reduce cost, and advance your organization's sustainability targets.

These continued objectives focus on implementing strategies and influencing stakeholders. You will learn how to implement automated schedules for non-production instances to eliminate idle energy use during off-hours, and how to use lifecycle policies to shift cold data into more efficient storage classes. You will practice using AWS Compute Optimizer to find right-sizing opportunities and review its recommendations safely before changing instance types. You will explore the trade-offs between performance and efficiency, for example when Graviton instances provide better performance per watt but require validation for your workload. Finally, you will learn how to present sustainability metrics to stakeholders and align architecture work with corporate ESG goals. This includes using the Customer Carbon Footprint Tool to visualize historical and projected emissions. These skills let you act technically and build the business case for sustainable choices. Which implementation will you pilot first: automated schedules, lifecycle rules, or a Compute Optimizer review?

Sustainable architecture means designing, building, and operating cloud workloads with the explicit goal of minimizing environmental impact. That is more than a slogan: it means treating energy and data movement as design metrics alongside cost and latency. Architecturally, it starts with the principle 'use only the resources you need, when you need them.' Practically, that yields actions like right-sizing instances, scheduling non-production shutdowns, and choosing managed or serverless services that avoid idle power draw. A concrete example is a development environment that runs only during business hours. When you schedule those instances to stop overnight and on weekends, the instances consume no energy during those periods, producing immediate savings in both emissions and cost. A common misconception is that sustainability always requires expensive new hardware or complex change. In truth, many high-impact steps are operational: trimming unused snapshots, enabling S3 lifecycle transitions, and applying Compute Optimizer recommendations. Key takeaway: sustainability is measurable and actionable. Ask yourself: which idle resources in your account are easy candidates for shutdown or right-sizing this week? Sustainable Architecture — Definition and Relevance means sustainable architecture treats energy, data movement, and idle resources as first-class design concerns and applies practical patterns to reduce impact.. Right-sizing and automated schedules are among the highest-impact operational steps architects can take. Start by collecting usage metrics such as C P U, memory, and network input and output over a representative period. Tools like AWS Compute Optimizer can analyze those metrics and propose smaller instance types when appropriate. A safe process is: identify candidates, simulate or test recommendations in non-production, and then apply changes during low-impact windows. For non-production environments that are only in use during business hours, implement automated shutdown and startup schedules. This can be done with scheduling tooling or simple automation that stops instances at night and restarts them in the morning. A concrete scenario: a t3. xlarge left running with low utilization for several days becomes a candidate for t3. medium or to be scheduled off when idle. The misconception to avoid is treating Compute Optimizer recommendations as automatic — always validate application behavior and performance after a change. Key takeaway: combine metrics, automated schedules, and safe validation to reduce running hours and energy consumption while preserving reliability. Choosing power-efficient instance types affects both performance and environmental impact. AWS offers ARM-based Graviton instances that often deliver better performance per watt than comparable x86 types. The practical decision requires workload validation. For C P U-bound workloads or highly parallel tasks, Graviton instances can provide similar or better throughput while consuming less energy for the same work. A contrasting scenario is software built and optimized only for x86 binaries; a migration could require recompilation or validation of libraries. A concrete example: an analytics service running many parallel worker processes may see improved throughput on M6g or C6g instances, translating into less runtime for the same job and therefore lower energy use. A common misconception is that switching is always a drop-in improvement. In reality, compatibility, performance profiles, and testing overhead matter. Key takeaway: consider Graviton for workloads that benefit from ARM architecture, but validate with benchmarks and performance testing so efficiency gains translate into real emissions reductions. Serverless computing contributes to sustainability by shifting responsibility for capacity and efficiency to the cloud provider. In the serverless model you pay and consume only when your code runs. This eliminates long-lived idle capacity and reduces energy waste tied to always-on servers. Services such as Lambda, SQS, SNS, and DynamoDB are managed and scaled by the provider, which can optimize placement and power usage across many tenants. A concrete example is an event-driven image processing pipeline that runs only when images arrive; with Lambda, there is no always-on worker consuming C P U between events. A common misconception is that serverless is always cheaper or faster; in some high-throughput, long-running tasks, other models may be more cost-effective. The key sustainability insight is that serverless improves utilization and reduces idle draw. When designing, consider throughput patterns, cold start characteristics, and whether your workload maps naturally to event-driven scaling. A reflective question: which components of your systems are best matched to serverless to reduce idle energy use? Data transfer and storage choices affect environmental impact because moving and storing data consumes energy. Start by minimizing cross-region and internet egress traffic where possible. Use caching and a content delivery network to reduce load on origin servers and avoid long-distance transfers. For storage, apply S3 intelligent tiering and lifecycle policies to transition objects to Glacier or Deep Archive as access patterns change. Deleting unnecessary data and old snapshots further reduces storage footprint and its associated energy cost. A concrete example is moving logs older than 90 days from S3 standard to Glacier Deep Archive, reducing the active storage footprint and the energy needed to replicate and maintain those objects. A common sustainable architecture pattern combines serverless compute, caching at the edge, and tiered storage to minimize runtime and data transfer energy. The pattern serves content through a CDN, uses serverless functions for on-demand processing, and stores archival content in lower-cost, lower-energy storage classes.
